At the software firm's open office in Kochi, Lakshmi had just been told the client's billing feature was due on the 28th. Before agreeing, she opened a notebook and drew the path from now to that date.
Coding: eight days. Testing: four days. But testing needed the client's sandbox, their test environment, and last time it had taken a full week to come through. She tapped the page. "If I ask for it when coding ends, testing starts a week late."
So she did two things that afternoon. First, she emailed the client's IT contact requesting the sandbox access immediately, and copied her manager, Chandrika. Second, she added two spare days before the 28th in the plan she shared, labelled plainly as "buffer for surprises".
Chandrika looked at the plan. "Why the buffer?"
"Because something always turns up."
The sandbox arrived six days later. Then a login bug took a day and a half. They delivered on the 27th.

qa.a: Chandrika, who questioned the buffer, likely sees its value once the login bug was absorbed without missing the date.

In the district town of Sagar, Mohit managed the software rollout for a mid-sized hospital. On Thursday he learned that go-live would be three weeks late. The lab machines' data wasn't matching the new system, and fixing the connection would take time.
He had to tell the hospital administrator, Dr Ritu, on Monday. His first impulse was to call right away and just say "delay". He stopped himself. She'll ask why. She'll ask when. She'll ask what it means for patients.
So he spent Friday preparing. The cause, in one sentence: the lab machines send results in an older format. The new date: 14 August. And two ideas to soften the blow: keep the old lab system running in parallel until then, and move the outpatient module live on the original date, since it didn't depend on lab data.
On Monday, Dr Ritu listened, frowned, then said, "Thank you for coming with a plan." They chose both options.

Nadia worked as an account lead for a small software firm in Lisbon, and on a Wednesday she found out the new patient records system for a private hospital would go live three weeks late. The data migration from the old system had hit corrupted files.
Her colleague Lucia said, "Call them now, get it over with."
Nadia shook her head. "If I call now, all I can say is 'sorry, it's late'. They'll ask why, and what now, and I won't know."
So she spent the afternoon getting answers. From the engineers: the cause, corrupted files in the older records, and how long cleaning them would take. From that: a new date, 2 October. I'm Santosh, and I share a cabin with Arnab at the consulting firm. The evening before he had to tell a retail client their new inventory system would be a month late, I watched him prepare.
He didn't write the bad news. He wrote the reactions. On a notepad, three headings: "They're angry." "Whose fault is it?" "Can we get a discount?"
Under each, he wrote a reply and read it out quietly, testing it. "I understand this is frustrating. Here's exactly what caused it." Then, "The delay came from our testing of their old data. We should have flagged it sooner. I'm not going to blame anyone on your side." Then, "I can't agree to a discount on this call, but I'll take it to my director today and come back to you by Friday."
He practised until his voice stayed level. I don't know how nervous he was inside, but the next morning, on the call, he never promised anything he couldn't keep.

I'm Pradeep, and I work on Elizabeth's team at the analytics firm. When our data platform for a bank client went down for two days, Elizabeth had to explain it to them. She had led the team for only six months.
I saw her in the corridor that morning, notebook in hand. "I don't know how much to tell them," she said, mostly to herself. "Do I explain the whole failure chain? Do I offer something?"
She booked fifteen minutes with our director. When she came back, she told us what they'd decided. Tone: honest and direct, full cause, no jargon. And yes, offer a service credit for the two days. The director would also join the call, to show the bank this was being taken seriously.
On the call, Elizabeth explained what happened and what had changed. The director offered the credit. The bank's head of IT said, "We appreciate you both being here."
I don't know how nervous she was, but her voice never wavered.
